Your strawberry frosting containing FD&C Red No. 3 must stop being manufactured with that color additive by January 15, 2027. On that date, the removal of 21 CFR 74.303 (the listing authorizing FD&C Red No. 3 in food) takes effect, and all existing certificates for batches of FD&C Red No. 3 cease to be effective for use in food (90 FR 4628; 91 FR 50475). The administrative stay that was in place from February 18, 2025, was lifted on August 5, 2026, and the January 15, 2027 effective date was confirmed (91 FR 50475).

Regarding product already on shelves: The January 2025 order explicitly states that '[w]hen FD&C Red No. 3 has been used in food or ingested drugs while its certificate is still effective, such food or ingested drugs will not be regarded as adulterated by reason of the use of such color additive' (90 FR 4628). This means frosting manufactured and containing FD&C Red No. 3 that was incorporated while the certificate was still effective (i.e., before January 15, 2027) is NOT adulterated and may remain on shelves and be sold after that date. Only use of FD&C Red No. 3 after its certificate ceases to be effective (i.e., incorporating it into food on or after January 15, 2027) would render the food adulterated.

Note: The January 2025 order sets no separate compliance date; the operative deadline is derived from the effective date of January 15, 2027. There is no phase-out period beyond that date for manufacturing.

response.answer:
Under the updated 'healthy' nutrient content claim rule (89 FR 106064, codified at 21 CFR 101.65(d)), a food that does not qualify for one of the automatic exemptions (e.g., single-ingredient foods from encouraged food groups, or water/tea/coffee) must meet two main criteria to bear the 'healthy' claim:

1. **Food Group Equivalent (FGE) requirement**: The food must contain a specified amount of at least one food group equivalent from the food groups encouraged by the Dietary Guidelines (vegetables, fruits, whole grains, fat-free or low-fat dairy, lean meat/seafood/eggs/beans/peas/lentils/nuts/seeds). The specific FGE amounts vary by product category (individual food, mixed product, main dish, or meal) as set forth in 21 CFR 101.65(d)(3)(ii)–(v) and the associated tables. (21 CFR 101.65(d)(2)–(3); 89 FR 106064)

2. **Nutrient-to-Limit (NTL) requirement**: The food must not exceed specified limits for added sugars, saturated fat, and sodium, expressed as a percentage of the Daily Value for these nutrients. These limits also vary by product category. (21 CFR 101.65(d)(3)(ii)–(v); 89 FR 106064; see also 90 FR 10592 at passage describing the rule as requiring 'FGEs and specific limits for added sugars, saturated fat, and sodium based on a percentage of the Daily Value for these nutrients')

As summarized in the background section of 90 FR 10592 (Doc. 2025-03118): the rule 'requires that, to bear a claim subject to the rule, individual food products, mixed products, main dishes, and meals must meet FGEs and specific limits for added sugars, saturated fat, and sodium based on a percentage of the Daily Value for these nutrients.'

response.answer: The 'healthy' implied nutrient content claim is governed by 21 CFR 101.65(d). This section defines the general nutritional claims paragraph covering labeling claims that are implied nutrient content claims because they suggest that a food may help consumers maintain healthy dietary practices due to its nutrient content. The general framework for implied nutrient content claims (including 'healthy') is set out in 21 CFR 101.13(b)(2)(ii), which defines an implied nutrient content claim as one that 'suggests that a food, because of its nutrient content, may be useful in maintaining healthy dietary practices, where there is also implied or explicit information about the nutrition content of the food (e.g., "healthy")' (21 CFR 101.13(b)(2)(ii) as revised by document 2024-29957, 89 FR 106064). The specific criteria a food must meet to bear the 'healthy' claim are found in 21 CFR 101.65(d). The final rule updating the definition of 'healthy' was published on December 27, 2024 (89 FR 106064, document 2024-29957), with an effective date of April 28, 2025 (as delayed by document 2025-03118), and a compliance date of February 25, 2028.

response.answer:
No, that was not a fair reading in mid-2025, and it is definitively incorrect now.

**What was true in mid-2025:** The January 2025 order revoking FD&C Red No. 3 (90 FR 4628, published 2025-01-16, Doc. 2025-00830) was subject to an automatic administrative stay under 21 U.S.C. 371(e)(2) as of February 18, 2025, triggered by the filing of objections. During that stay, the effective dates of January 15, 2027 (food uses, removal of 21 CFR 74.303) and January 18, 2028 (ingested drugs, removal of 21 CFR 74.1303) were suspended but not cancelled or moved. The order itself was a final binding order, not a proposal. An administrative stay does not mean a rule 'might never take effect'—it means the agency must evaluate the objections before the rule can proceed. The stated effective dates remained unconfirmed during the stay period, but the underlying legal determination (that FD&C Red No. 3 is deemed unsafe under the Delaney Clause) was already made in a final order (90 FR 4628 at 4631). Characterizing the revocation as 'not final' was incorrect; it was final but stayed.

**What is the position now:** FDA lifted the administrative stay on August 5, 2026 (91 FR 50475, Doc. 2026-15920). In that document, FDA overruled all objections, denied requests for a public hearing, and explicitly confirmed the effective dates of the January 2025 order. The document states: 'we are ending the administrative stay of the January 2025 order, and under the January 2025 order we are repealing the listing for FD&C Red No. 3 in § 74.303 as a color additive in food and § 74.1303 as a color additive in ingested drugs effective January 15, 2027, and January 18, 2028, respectively' (91 FR 50475). This constitutes 'final action on the objections' under section 701(e)(2) of the FD&C Act.

The revocation is therefore fully confirmed and binding:
- **Food uses (21 CFR 74.303):** Effective January 15, 2027. After that date, use of FD&C Red No. 3 in food renders the food adulterated (90 FR 4628).
- **Ingested drug uses (21 CFR 74.1303):** Effective January 18, 2028.

No compliance date was separately stated; the operative deadlines are derived from the effective dates (Doc. 2025-00830). There is no remaining legal mechanism pending that could prevent these dates from taking effect.

- Instruction 3: Revise § 74.1303 to incorporate identity and specifications previously cross-referenced from § 74.303 (effective January 15, 2027).
- Instruction 4: Remove § 74.1303 (effective January 18, 2028).

The order sets no separate compliance date for any provision. The deadlines are derived from the effective dates: once § 74.303 is removed on January 15, 2027, food containing FD&C Red No. 3 is adulterated; once § 74.1303 is removed on January 18, 2028, ingested drugs containing FD&C Red No. 3 are adulterated (2025-00830#0021; timeline-facts).

An administrative stay under 21 U.S.C. 371(e)(2) was in effect from February 18, 2025, through August 5, 2026, but FDA lifted the stay and confirmed both effective dates unchanged (91 FR 50475, Doc. 2026-15920#0000).

response.answer: Under 21 CFR 101.65(a)(2), a 'healthy' implied nutrient content claim must be made in accordance with the general requirements for nutrient content claims in § 101.13, with one specific carve-out: § 101.13(h) is excepted when the nutrient content claim is made in accordance with paragraph (d) of § 101.65. Section 101.13(h) is the disclosure requirement that would otherwise mandate a statement such as 'See nutrition information for ___ content' when a food exceeds specified levels of fat, saturated fat, cholesterol, or sodium. This disclosure requirement does not apply to foods bearing the 'healthy' claim under § 101.65(d). All other provisions of § 101.13 — including requirements on claim type size (§ 101.13(f)), the general prohibition on nutrient content claims unless made in accordance with subpart D (§ 101.13(b)), and the requirement that the food be labeled with nutrition information — remain applicable.

response.answer: Yes, your shelf-stable lentil soup labeled 'healthy' is affected by the updated definition of the term 'healthy' under the final rule published at 89 FR 106064 (Doc. 2024-29957, published 2024-12-27). Until that compliance date, you may continue to use the 'healthy' claim under the prior criteria, but you must comply with the new requirements by February 25, 2028.

However, the absence of a compliance date does NOT mean there is no hard deadline. Once the effective date arrives, the listing in 21 CFR 74.303 is removed, and any food containing FD&C Red No. 3 becomes adulterated as a matter of law. The operative deadline is therefore derived from the effective date: January 15, 2027 for food uses (all provisions except amendatory instruction 4), and January 18, 2028 for ingested drug uses (removal of 21 CFR 74.1303). After January 15, 2027, food products colored with Red No. 3 — including existing inventory — would be adulterated regardless of when they were manufactured or labeled.

Note: An administrative stay under 21 U.S.C. 371(e)(2) was in effect from February 18, 2025 through August 5, 2026 (per Doc. 2026-15920). That stay has now expired. Importantly, a stay does not move dates day-for-day; it merely suspends the provision during the stay period. The timeline facts confirm the stay is no longer in force ('in_force_now': false) and that 'dates_changed': false. Therefore, the January 15, 2027 effective date for food uses remains operative.

In summary: there is a hard deadline — it is January 15, 2027 for foods — derived from the effective date. It is not a stated 'compliance date,' but it functions as the real deadline after which the color additive is no longer authorized and products containing it are adulterated.
